ROLL OF HONOR No. XXII. 


QUARTERMASTER GENERAL'S OFFICE, 
. Washington, D. C., August 4, 1869. 
The following Roll of Honor, prepared in the cemeterial branch of 
this office, under the direction of Brevet Brigadier General Alex. J. 
Perry, Quartermaster U. S. A., and containing the record of sixteen 
thousand four hundred and eighty-five (16,485) graves of deceased 
Union soldiers interred in the national cemetery at Nashville, Tennessee, 
is published by authority of the Secretary of War, for the information 
of their surviving comrades and friends. 
M. C. MEIGS, 
Quartermaster General, Brevet Major General U.S. A.

QUARTERMASTER GENERAL'S OFFICE, 
Washington, D. C., July 31, 1869, 
GENERAL: I have the honor to submit herewith for publication (as 
the twenty-second volume of the Rolls of Honor) the record of sixteen 
thousand four hundred and eighty-five (16,485) graves of deceased Union 
soldiers interred in the national cemetery at Nashville, Tennessee. The 
remains of twelve thousand four hundred and eighty-six (42,486) of these 
are identified; and while those of three thousand nine hundred and 
ninety-nine (5.999) are classed as “ Unknown,” yetalistis hereto appended 
showing the names of four thousand four hundred and seventy-two (4,472) 
Union soldiers who are known to have died or were killed at Nashville, Ten- 
nessee, and different points in the vicinity, and who have either been 
interred as ‘* Unknown” in this cemetery, or have been removed to their 
homes by relatives and friends. 
I am, General, very respectfully, your obedient servant, 
ALEX. J. PERRY, 
Brev. Brig. General, and Quartermaster U.S. A. 
Brevet Major General M. C. MEIGs, 
Quartermaster General U, S. A., Washington, D. C.

NASHVILLE NATIONAL CEMETERY, 





This cemetery is situated on the Gallatin pike, six miles from Nash- 
ville, Tennessee, and is intersected by the Louisville and Nashville rail- 
road, which divides it into nearly equal parts. It comprises about 
fifty-eight acres of beautifully undwating ground, a part of which is 
covered with a grove of stately forest trees. The avenues, nearly four 
miles in extent, are macadamized and graveled so as to form pleasant 
and delightful drives. A natural rivwet running through the grounds 
has been widened and deepened, and neatly walled up to form an outlet 
for drainage, as well as to serve as an ornamental water-course. The 
whole grounds are surrounded by a substantial picket fence. 

The total number of dead interred in the cemetery is sixteen thousand 
four hundred and eighty-six, of which twelve thousand four hundred 
and eighty-seven are known, and three thousand nine hundred and 
ninety-nine unknown, Of white soldiers there are fourteen thousand 
five hundred and seventy-seven, and of colored one thousand nine hun- 
dred and nine. The number of regiments represented is seven hundred 
and thirty, and of States and independent organizations thirty-one. 

The bodies interred in this cemetery have been gathered from an 
extensive region of country, along the Cumberland River from Carthage 
on the east to Clarksville on the west; from the line of the Louisville 
and Nashville railroad as far as Mumfordsville, Kentucky; from the 
Nashville and Northwestern railroad to the Tennessee River at John- 
sonville; from the Edgefield and Kentucky and the Memphis branch of 
the Louisville and Nashvillerailroad; from Bowling Green to Clarksville ; 
from the Nashville and Chattanooga railroad to Lavergne; and from all 
intermediate and adjacent country; from the Nashville battle-field, and 
many of the skirmish grounds in Southern Kentucky, comprising those 
originally collected and buried at Tompkinsville. 

The number of distinct burial places from which these bodies were 
taken is two hundred and fifty-one. 

A very large proportion of the dead in this cemetery, however, were 
transferred from the hospital burial grounds in and around the city of 
Nashville. 

A full and complete record of all the interments in this cemetery, 
together with a complete copy of all burial sheets, has been deposited 
at the cemetery for the information of friends and visitors. 

Plats of the cemetery, showing the arrangements of the grounds and 
the precise location of each grave, with the number toeach, will be found 
on deposit in the office of the Quartermaster General, at Washington, 
and also a duplicate copy of the burial sheets. 

Persons desiring to visit this cemetery can reach it by railroad from 
Louisville or Nashville, stopping at Madison station, or by private con- 
veyance from Nashville over the Gallatin pike. 

The superintendent in charge of this cemetery may be addressed 
through the Nashville post office.

ROLL OF HONOR No. XXIII. 


QUARTERMASTER GENERAL'S OFFICE, 
Washington, D. C., August 5, 1869. 
The following Roll of Honor, prepared in the cemeterial branch of 
this office, under the direction of Brevet Brigadier General Alexander 
J. Perry, quartermaster United States army, and containing the records 
of the graves of sixteen thousand six hundred and seventy-five (16,675) 
Union soldiers interred in the national cemeteries at Marietta, Georgia; 
Fort Donelson, (Dover,) Tennessee, and (supplementary to No. XI of 
the Rolls of Honor) Chattanooga, Murfreesboro’, (Stone’s River,) and 
Knoxville, Tennessee, is published by authority of the Secretary of 
War, for the information of their surviving comrades and friends. 
M. C. MEIGS, 
(@uartermaster General, Brevet Major General U.S. A.

QUARTERMASTER GENERAL’S OFFICE, 
Washington, D. C., July 31, 1869. 
GENERAL: I have the honor to submit herewith for publication, as 
the twenty-third number of the Rolls of Honor, the record of the graves 
of sixteen thousand six hundred and seventy-five (16,675) Union soldiers 
interred in the national cemeteries at Marietta, Georgia; Fort Donelson, 
Tennessee; Chattanooga, Tennessee; Murfreesboro’, (Stone’s River,) 
Tennessee, and Knoxville, Tennessee. The records from the last three 
cemeteries are supplementary to those heretofore published in No. XI 
of the Rolls of Honor, and complete the lists of names of those cemeteries. 
I am, General, very respectfully, your obedient servant, 
ALEX. J. PERRY, 
Brev. Brig. General, and Quartermaster U.S. A. 
Brevet Major General M. C. MEIGS, 
Quartermaster General U. S. A., Washington, D. C,

MARIETTA AND ATLANTA NATIONAL CEMETERY, 


The Marietta and Atlanta National Cemetery is located in the out- 
skirts of the village of Marietta, Georgia, in full view of the Kenesaw 
Mountain, twenty miles from Atlanta, on the line of the Western and 
Atlantic railroad. It covers twenty-four acres, and was donated to 
the United States by Mr. Henry G. Cole, of Marietta. The ground rises 
gradually from all sides, and the summit near the center of the cemetery 
commands an extensive view of the surrounding country. It is beauti- 
fully laid out in sections, and is intersected with winding walks and 
avenues, macadamized and graveled. , 

From the summit now daily floats the national ensign, and around it 
lie, in solemn repose, nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-four Union 
dead, whose remains have been gathered from all the battle-fields and 
hospital grounds of Sherman’s advance upon Atlanta, from the banks 
of the Oostanaula, at Resaca, to Jonesboro, below Atlanta, and east to 
Augusta. The dead from Central Alabama, at first collected and interred 
at Montgomery, have also been transferred to this cemetery. Here Bite 
those who fell with MePherson at Atlanta, with Harker at Kenesa 
on the fields of Peachtree Creek, and in the forests of New Hope Chureh. 
and here, too, lie those martyr heroes who so freely sacrificed their lives 
on the heights of Allatoona. 

This Roll of Honor has been made up from the burial sheets forwarded 
to the office of the chief quartermaster of the Department of the Cum- 
berland for use in the preparation of the Roll of Honor. The entire list 
has been subjected to careful examination and correction by comparison 
with the original muster rolls of the several States. 

Many names accredited to a State are not to be found upon the rolls 
of the organizations to which they purport to belong. Such, in all cases, 
are designated by a star (*), and must be left for future research. 

The interments in this cemetery are now completed, and a superin- 
tendent has been appointed by the Secretary of War.

CUMBERLAND RIVER NATIONAL CEMETERY, FORT 
DONELSON, TENNESSEE, 


This cemetery occupies the site of the new fort erected subsequent to 
the battle of Fort Donelson, half a mile below the village of Dover. 
The site was selected by a board consisting of Chaplain W. b. Earnshaw, 
Major A. W. Wills, A. Q. M., and Captain G. W. Marshall, A. Q. M. 

The original design, to collect at this point not only those who fell at 
the batile of Fort Donelson but all who were interred on the banks of 
the Cumberland from Smithland to Clarksville, was abandoned after 
the purchase of the ground and the laying out of the cemetery, and it 
now contains only those who were found upon the battle-field, and from 
a small territory adjacent, and from a few towns in the border counties 
of Kentucky. The total number is six hundred and seventy, of which 
one hundred and fifty-eight are known and five hundred and twelve 
are unknown. 

The entire tract of fifteen acres is surrounded with a picket fence, 
and that portion immediately occupied by the graves has been inclosed 
by a stone wall. 

This cemetery contains the largest regimental group of any cemetery 
in the department. In the battle of Fort Donelson, sixty-two men of 
the eleventh regiment Illinois infantry, reported to have fallen in resist- 
ing the attempt of General Forrest to cut his way. out, were buried in 
one trench upon the battle-field. A full list of their names is appended 
to the roll, but the separate bodies, except in two instances, have not 
been identified. 

The cemetery may be reached by boat from Smithland or Nashville, 
or by Memphis and Charleston railroad, stopping at Stewart’s station 
and procuring private conveyance thirteen miles to the cemetery. 

The superintendent in charge of this cemetery may be addressed at 
Dover, Tennessee.

CHATTANOOGA NATIONAL CEMETERY. 


(ADDITIONAL TO VOLUME XI.) 


* 

This Roll of Honor of additional dead interred in the Chattanooga 
National Cemetery contains a record of three thousand two hundred 
and sixty-two interments made since the publication of General Orders 
No. 96, Quartermaster General’s Office, December 11, 1866, (Roll of 
Honor No. 11,) and completes the record of all interments in that cem- 
etery. It comprises the dead removed from the pest hospital at Chat- 
tanooga, and the remains of those who were originally buried at 
Bridgeport, Stevenson, Huntsville, and along the line of the Memphis 
and Charleston railroad to the crossing of the Tennessee River at 
Decatur, and generally through all parts of Northern Alabama. By 
reference to the recapitulation, in which the interments before reported 
are recounted, it appears that the total number of interments in this 
cemetery is twelve thousand eight hundred and sixty-three, of which 
seven thousand nine hundred and thirty-six are known and four thou- 
sand nine hundred and twenty-seven unknown. This is the total num- 
ber of interments to this date. A few scattered dead are known to 
have been overlooked in the original search, who will eventually be 
removed to this cemetery. 

The number of unknown dead is here simply given in the aggregate 
without the designation of section or grave, but on the record kept at 
this cemetery each unknown grave, as well as the known, is designated 
by its proper section and number. 

The cemetery is now fully completed, with a permanent stone wall 
inclosing it, and four siege-gun monuments have been erected on the 
summit of the central hill around the flag-staff. 

A superintendent is in charge.

Note.—The total (12,863) excteds the actual number of interments in this cemetery by _ 
7, which is accounted for by the fact that 7 bodies have been disinterred by friends and the 
graves refilled with other bodies, the original name not having been erased from the records. 

In the original Roll of Honor No. XI, 2,305 unknown dead reported by the superintend- 
ent in the aggregate, without section or number of grave, were inadvertently added to the 
17 unknown in the list of miscellaneous—with section and number of grave given—and 
reported as 2,322 miscellaneous unknown. 


STONE’S RIVER NATIONAL CEMETERY, MURFREES- 
| BORO, TENNESSEE, 


(ADDITIONAL TO NO. XI.) 


The following supplementary Roll of Honor completes the record of 
interments in the Stone’s River Cemetery. It comprises 1,359 bodies 
removed from the Rose Hill Cemetery, at Columbia, Tennessee, the 
dead from the pest hospital at Murfreesboro, and a few scattered bodies 
in the surrounding country overlooked in the original search. Among 
those removed from Columbia are the dead from the Franklin battle- 
field, and from Spring Hill and other points on the Nashville and Decatur 
railroad. 

The Franklin dead occupy a section by themselves, which is desig- 
nated as the Franklin section. 

Since the publication of the former roll, this cemetery has been 
entirely completed, and is now in charge of a superintendent. 

The combined recapitulation shows the number now interred in this 
cemetery to be 6,124.

KNOXVILLE NATIONAL CEMETERY, 


(ADDITIONAL TO VOL, XL.) 


The following supplementary Roll of Honor completes, in connection 
with those published in General Orders No. 96, Quartermaster General’s 
Office, December 11, 1866, the records of all interments made in the 
Knoxville National Cemetery, and shows the total number to be three 
thousand one hundred and sixty-three. 

This list comprises the interments of one thousand two hundred and 
fifty-six deceased Union soldiers, between five and six hundred of which 
were originally gathered from portions of Kentucky, Virginia, and Ten- 
nessee, in the vicinity of Cumberland Gap, and interred in a national 
cemetery temporarily established at that place. The interments are 
now all completed, and the cemetery is finished and in charge of a 
superintendent. 

The cemetery is situated one mile from the center of Knoxville, in a 
northwesterly direction, on the Jacksboro pike and on the Knoxville 
and Kentucky railroad, about one-half of a mile north from the joint 
depots of the East Tennessee and Virginia and East Tennessee and 
Georgia railroads, and about two hundred yards west of the road lead- 
ing north from those depots, called Broadway. 

It contains about ten acres, and is laid out in the form of a square, 
the graves being arranged in concentric circles around a mound in the 
middle of the square, whereon is erected a flagstaff, from which float the 
national colors. 


301 


KNOXVILLE NATIONAL CEMETERY, TENNESSEE.
